title.rendered: GTA 6 vehicle customization: Every detail revealed so far

content.rendered:
GTA 6 Extended Look finally hit Netflix last week and gave fans a plethora of different reasons to be excited about the highly anticipated title, scheduled to come out on November 19, 2026. From the stupefyingly lively world of Vice City to the highly detailed and highly customized vehicles, the nearly half-hour-long showcase contained lots of intriguing new visuals.

Speaking of vehicle customization, cars turned out to be one of the more notable highlights from the first look at GTA 6’s gameplay. Things such as heavily modded cars and race cars were given a short but prominent place in the video. Below, we have compiled all the details about GTA 6’s cars, car customization, and car-related side missions that you may have missed.

All car customization features in GTA 6

  1. Cars have a wide variety of decals that can be put on spots like the back glass.
  2. There is the option to mod underglow onto the car’s bottom surface.
  3. Various liveries are available in mod shops, including liveries that glow in the dark.
  4. The flames coming out of the exhaust pipes can be color-customized.
  5. The lighting on the number plate is customizable with different colors.
  6. Lug nuts on the rim of a wheel can be changed in terms of color.
  7. An interior LED strip can be placed on the inside of the back glass.
  8. The interior lighting of cars can be customized.

Through the GTA 6 leaks we saw last month, we already had received a good look at cars and driving in the game. However, the Extended Look has shown the true level of detail and customization that will be possible when you set foot in Vice City.

Besides the gas stations being able to repair your vehicle, you can also take them to Pay N’ Spray, a series staple, to do certain modifications such as a new paint job. However, extensive modifications would be available through dedicated mod shops, some of which are controversially exclusive to those who order GTA 6’s Ultimate Edition.

Cars in GTA 6: What changed since GTA 5

  1. The driving in GTA 6 appears to feel heavier than in GTA 5, with the car weight substantially coming into play during turns and quick movements.
  2. The car interior is highly detailed, complete with buttons on the car door, backseat armrest strap and even the airbag warning sticker.
  3. On the outside, the headlights of cars now have daytime running lights (DRLs).
  4. The underside of the chassis also has 3D details instead of 2D textures, as was the case in GTA 5.
  5. Car damage is apparently more specific, with individual parts showing signs of damage.
  6. The indicator on the rear lights now works according to the turns you take.
  7. NPC cars can also sport a heavily customized look more often than usual.
  8. Apart from acting as your transport, cars now also double up as storage, with the trunk being used to store items such as firearms in GTA 6.

These changes are understandably being implemented to enhance the realism in the GTA sequel. With that said, fans can expect the days of arcade-y car handling and physics-defying car jumps in the franchise to be numbered as the game’s launch draws near.

Vehicle-based activities in GTA 6

The Extended Look revealed a variety of different side activities in GTA 6, ranging from basketball to base jumping. In addition, there were a few vehicle-based activities on display as well. The video confirmed that illegal street racing, car racing, and off-road racing are set to be part of the forthcoming title.

Since past GTA titles have included racing as a significant part of its side content, it’s not surprising that the new GTA is also following in the footsteps and doing the same. It will be interesting to see how these activities increase in difficulty with the new car handling and weightiness incorporated into Rockstar’s title.

Rounding up

Fans are certainly thrilled by what GTA 6 Extended Look had to show them, as evident by the video on Rockstar’s official YouTube channel amassing 1.5 million likes, at the time of writing, in about 11 days. It not only gave the community a long-awaited deeper look at GTA 6’s gameplay but also injected more hype into it by giving a glimpse at the level of meticulous work Rockstar Games devs have once again done this time around.

After shipping two monumental open-world action-adventure titles in 2013’s GTA 5 and 2018’s Red Dead Redemption 2, it will be exciting to see all that the GTA makers have prepared for fans to experience this year. Overtaking those two behemoths of a hit might generally be considered a tall order for any game, but judging by what experts have been saying, GTA 6 seems to be fairly up to the task.

Don’t miss these related reads:

  • GTA 6 map comparison: How much bigger is Vice City than GTA 5’s Los Santos
  • Every GTA protagonist, ranked from worst to best
  • Why GTA 6 needs a first-person mode

title.rendered: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 leak points to four new features

content.rendered:
Code in the watchOS 27 and iOS 27 betas may have revealed four changes coming to Apple’s next watches. A MacRumors forum post from user pdfu points to a new Readiness app, more detailed strength-workout tracking, a revised optical-sensing system, and possible 128GB storage.

Apple has not confirmed any of them. The clues also do not prove that every feature will arrive on both the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

A new Readiness app may sit beside Workout

The beta code refers to a separate Apple Watch app called Readiness. It appears in the watchOS launcher logic and in the iPhone Watch app’s code for arranging the default Home Screen, where it sits next to Workout.

That name suggests a broader recovery or wellness view, separate from the existing Vitals app. The code does not explain what data Readiness would show or whether it would be exclusive to the new watches.

Strength workouts could track each set

Apple is also preparing health data structures that can store more detail about strength training. The fields include individual sets, repetitions, weight, equipment, body side, and workout duration.

That would give the Workout app a better record of how a session was performed instead of treating strength training as one broad activity. The code points to the data model, not a finished screen or a confirmed watchOS 27 feature.

The optical sensor may get a hardware update

Another clue is a sensor family called "Sunstone4p0." The code describes lower noise coefficients and channel selection based on the watch’s position and orientation.

In plain terms, that could help the watch choose a better sensing path when the reflected pulse signal is weak or when the watch sits differently on the wrist. It may point to revised heart-sensing hardware, but the code does not identify the final component or the model that will use it.

128GB storage is possible, not guaranteed

The code also contains a NAND storage profile tied to the T8320 chip that is associated with the Series 12 and Ultra 4. That has led to speculation that Apple could double Apple Watch storage from 64GB to 128GB.

The benefit would be more room for music, offline content, apps, and future on-device features. Most buyers probably will not need that much space, though, and the storage profile does not prove that Apple will offer 128GB on every configuration. A current Apple Watch buying guide shows how the existing lineup is positioned today.

The launch is still unconfirmed

Apple’s September 9 event is the likely place to learn whether these features are real. Separate reporting has also tied the event to the Series 12 and Ultra 4, including another Apple Watch Ultra 4 rumor about sensors and health alerts.

Until Apple shows the watches or publishes their specifications, the safest read is that the beta code reveals what the company is testing, not what every customer will get.

title.rendered: WhatsApp may let users connect up to five third-party AI agents

content.rendered:
WhatsApp is testing a way to let users connect outside AI agents directly to chats in the app. The feature, spotted by WABetaInfo, lets users create a dedicated conversation for an agent, send it instructions, and receive replies without opening another app.

The feature is still limited to some Android beta users. WhatsApp has not announced a public rollout or an iPhone release.

How the agent chats would work

Users can add an agent from WhatsApp’s settings, give it a name, and choose a profile photo. WhatsApp then generates an API key that the user pastes into the service hosting the agent. Compatible services can use that connection to send messages back into the new WhatsApp chat.

WABetaInfo says the feature supports up to five agents per account. They could be AI agents, but the system also supports simpler bots that carry out specific commands. Each one appears as its own conversation, so users can keep different tools separate.

The agent only gets access to what the user shares in its chat. It cannot read other WhatsApp conversations, contacts, or media, and the current implementation does not support group chats or communities. Removing an agent disconnects it, but WhatsApp keeps the existing chat history visible.

These chats are not end-to-end encrypted

The privacy detail matters more than the five-agent limit. WhatsApp’s Help Center says chats with third-party agents are not considered end-to-end encrypted because a Meta service manages the conversation for the agent developer.

That does not give an agent access to the rest of your WhatsApp account. It does mean users should treat the dedicated chat differently from a normal conversation with another person. The agent developer can access the messages as part of the service, so sensitive information does not belong there unless the user trusts that provider.

WhatsApp also warns that AI responses may be inaccurate. That is worth keeping in mind when an agent is asked to make decisions or carry out tasks based on incomplete information.

The company has been adding more AI features to WhatsApp, including Incognito Chat for Meta AI and testing AI summaries for unread messages. Third-party agents take that shift a step further by letting people bring their own tools into the messaging app.

The rollout is still small

The feature appeared in WhatsApp beta for Android version 2.26.35.3 and is rolling out to a limited number of accounts in select countries. Most users will not see an Agents section in WhatsApp’s settings yet.

WhatsApp has not said when the feature will reach more Android accounts, group chats, or iPhone users. Until then, the useful takeaway is simple: agent chats may soon be easier to set up, but they will have a different privacy model from regular WhatsApp messages.

excerpt.rendered: WhatsApp is testing native chats for up to five third-party AI agents. The feature is limited on Android, and agent chats are not end-to-end encrypted.

title.rendered: Five iPhone 18 Pro camera features may be hidden in iOS 27 code

content.rendered:
Apple may be preparing five camera controls that have not appeared in the iOS 27 betas yet. A MacRumors forum post from user pdfu points to new Camera code for exposure scopes, focus tools, repeated self-timer shots, manual focus, and aperture-based image correction.

The code does not confirm that these features are coming to the iPhone 18 Pro. None is available in the current beta, and Apple could hold some back for a later update.

Five camera changes appear in the leak

The reported features cover both photo controls and the processing that happens after the shutter is pressed:

  1. Exposure scopes: The Camera app may add waveform and histogram views to help users judge brightness while shooting. The code includes luminance, RGB Composite, and RGB Parade options.
  2. Focus peaking and highlight warnings: Colored edges could show which parts of a scene are in focus. A separate overlay could warn when bright areas are losing detail, using solid colors, pulses, diagonal stripes, or a checkerboard pattern.
  3. Repeated self-timer shots: A timer could take several photos in a row, restarting the countdown without waiting for each image to finish processing. That would be useful for group photos and moving into position without running back to the phone after every shot.
  4. Manual focus: A slider could let users set and lock focus instead of leaving the job entirely to autofocus. Apple already offers a similar control in Final Cut Camera.
  5. Aperture-based image correction: iOS 27 could choose different lens-correction data depending on the camera’s aperture setting, then blend between nearby calibration points.

The aperture code is the clearest iPhone 18 Pro clue

The last feature fits a separate iPhone 18 Pro rumor. Apple is widely expected to add a variable-aperture main camera, which would let the lens opening change instead of staying fixed. If that hardware arrives, the new processing code could help the Camera app compensate for how the lens behaves at different settings.

The forum post says the system can use up to four calibration references. That does not mean the iPhone will have four physical aperture stops. It only describes how iOS can select and blend correction data.

The same product cycle has already produced leaks about the lineup and chip. iOS 27 beta code is believed to reference the fall iPhone 18 Pro models and Apple’s foldable, while a separate A20 Pro leak points to a possible seven-core GPU. Those reports are also unconfirmed.

Apple may reveal more this week

Apple’s September 9 event is the first obvious chance to show the iPhone 18 Pro camera system. Still, a feature appearing in beta code does not guarantee a launch-day release. The controls could remain hidden, be limited to new hardware, or arrive in a later iOS 27 update.

For now, the leak suggests Apple is working on more serious camera controls for the iPhone. It does not yet tell us which of them will actually ship.

title.rendered: I compared the Pixel 11 Pro XL with the Galaxy S26 Ultra: Which one is better for everyday use?

content.rendered:
The Pixel 11 Pro XL and Galaxy S26 Ultra are two of the best flagship Android phones you can buy right now, but choosing between them isn’t as simple as comparing specs.

Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra has a faster processor, more versatile cameras, an S Pen, and a long list of features. The Pixel 11 Pro XL takes a different approach, focusing on clean software, smarter AI features, and a camera experience.

That got me thinking: which one is actually better to use every day? After all, most of us don’t spend our day running benchmark tests. We take photos, scroll social media, watch videos, answer calls, use AI, and expect our phones to last until bedtime.

So, instead of turning this into another spec-sheet battle, I compared the Pixel 11 Pro XL and the Galaxy S26 Ultra based on what actually matters in daily life. Here’s the one I think comes out on top.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Specs at a glance

Before getting into the experience, here is how the two Android flagships compare on paper.

On paper, the Galaxy S26 Ultra looks like the obvious winner. But specs don’t tell the whole story.

Design and build quality: Which one feels better in my hand?

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is lighter at 214g, despite having the slightly larger 6.9-inch display. Samsung has also made the Ultra thinner than some of its predecessors, measuring 7.9mm.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL is technically thinner at 7.6mm, but it weighs more at 227g. However, it feels better in hand thanks to the rounded corners and satin matte glass on the back. I especially like Google’s horizontal camera bar approach. It distributes the camera hardware across the phone and reduces annoying table wobbles.

Google has also reduced the size of the camera bar on the Pixel 11 Pro XL for a more refined look. Then there is HiLight, Google’s new LED feature integrated into the camera area. It can visually interact with certain features and notifications, giving the Pixel a little personality.

That said, if I wanted a phone that screams “most expensive Android available,” I would probably pick the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Samsung’s industrial design feels more premium and deliberate. The integrated S Pen also gives the phone something the Pixel simply cannot replicate.

My design verdict: I would choose the Pixel 11 Pro XL for comfort and personality, whereas the Galaxy S26 Ultra for premium hardware and productivity.

Display: I used both screens for movies, gaming, and scrolling

Both phones have excellent displays.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL uses a 6.8-inch Super Actua LTPO OLED display with a dynamic refresh rate up to 120Hz and peak brightness reaching up to 3,600 nits. Samsung goes slightly bigger with a 6.9-inch Dynamic AMOLED display with HDR10+.

For movies, YouTube, social media, and gaming, I don’t think either screen will disappoint. But Samsung has introduced something much more interesting than another brightness number.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra features a built-in Privacy Display designed to make the screen harder to see from certain angles. This sounds unnecessary until I am using my phone on a train, aeroplane, in an office, or in a crowded café. However, I noticed that it reduces screen clarity.

After testing both displays for scrolling, streaming, reading, and gaming, I prefer the Pixel’s Super Actua display. It’s best when used under direct sunlight.

My display verdict: Pixel 11 Pro XL wins for the simpler, no-compromise viewing experience.

Performance: Tensor vs. Snapdragon in real life

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is the more powerful phone, and the benchmark numbers make that impossible to ignore.

Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra runs on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, while the Pixel 11 Pro XL uses Google’s Tensor G6 chip with Titan M3 security coprocessor. Google has improved Tensor performance over previous generations, but it still doesn’t compete with Qualcomm’s best silicon in raw CPU performance.

Geekbench 6 Results

The Galaxy S26 Ultra delivers higher raw power and sustained performance for AI processes and heavy workloads. However, the Pixel 11 Pro XL has more than enough performance for normal smartphone use.

Also, Google’s approach to Tensor has always been slightly different. Rather than chasing the highest benchmark numbers, Tensor is designed around Google’s AI features, computational photography, thermal management, and on-device processing. I would choose this if I cared more about how the software uses the processor’s raw power.

If you regularly play demanding games, edit videos, use intensive apps, or simply want the maximum possible performance, I would recommend going with the Galaxy S26 Ultra without a doubt.

Performance winner: Galaxy S26 Ultra

Software experience: Clean Android vs. feature-packed One UI

This might be the hardest section to score because it comes down to personality.

Google’s version of Android feels cleaner, more cohesive, and less cluttered. Features like Call Assist, spam protection, Recorder, voice typing, Live Translate, Pixel Screenshots, and Google’s AI tools feel connected rather than scattered across different menus.

Google also benefits from controlling Android itself. New Android features and Gemini integrations naturally feel at home on a Pixel. The Pixel 11 Pro XL ships with Android 17 and is supported by Google’s 7-year software update commitment.

Samsung’s One UI is arguably the most feature-packed Android interface available. And I mean that as both a compliment and a warning.

I get:

  • Advanced multitasking
  • Samsung DeX
  • Extensive customization
  • Good Lock modules
  • Floating windows
  • Deep ecosystem controls
  • Samsung Notes
  • Secure Folder
  • Modes and Routines

For a power user, One UI is incredible.

My software verdict: I prefer the Pixel for everyday simplicity and Samsung for productivity and customisation.

Gemini vs. Galaxy AI: Which is actually more useful?

I think the Pixel 11 Pro XL has its strongest argument here.

Certainly, Samsung has built one of the most comprehensive AI suites in smartphones. The Galaxy S26 Ultra combines Samsung’s own Galaxy AI features with Gemini integration, giving users access to writing tools, translation, search, productivity assistance, image editing, and contextual AI capabilities.

But I think Google has one important advantage. Gemini doesn’t feel like an AI feature. It increasingly feels like part of the operating system.

The Pixel’s AI toolkit includes features such as:

  • Gemini integration
  • Call Assist
  • Live Translate
  • Pixel Screenshots
  • Camera Coach
  • Magic Capture
  • Magic Editor
  • AI-powered photography tools
  • Proactive Gemini Intelligence assistance
  • Better voice typing

These are the kinds of features I can imagine using every day naturally.

However, I will give Samsung credit for something Google still doesn’t offer in the same way: greater control over AI processing. The Galaxy S26 Ultra can offer local processing options for certain AI features. For privacy-conscious users, that’s a major advantage.

Winner: I would choose Gemini on the Pixel for everyday usefulness.

Camera comparison: I took the same photos with both phones

Camera comparisons are where megapixel counts become almost meaningless.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra has the more intimidating hardware specifications:

  • 200MP main camera
  • 50MP ultra-wide
  • 10MP 3x telephoto
  • 50MP 5x telephoto

The Pixel 11 Pro XL takes a simpler but extremely capable approach:

  • 50MP main camera
  • 48MP ultra-wide with Macro Focus
  • 48MP 5x telephoto
  • 42MP autofocus selfie camera

Both phones offer advanced computational photography, high-resolution capture, long-range zoom, and AI-powered editing. But they approach photography differently.

The Pixel camera experience has historically been about pulling out the phone, pressing the shutter button, and trusting Google’s computational photography to do the rest.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL improves the camera hardware while adding a new image signal processor and features such as:

  • Magic Capture
  • Camera Looks
  • Camera Coach
  • Creator Suite
  • Faster Night Sight
  • Pro Zoom up to 120x
  • Macro Focus
  • Best Take
  • Add Me
  • Real Tone

Google’s camera advantage comes from knowing the phone understands what I’m trying to capture.

On the other hand, Samsung’s camera system is built around flexibility. The dual telephoto system gives me more options across different zoom ranges, while the 200MP main camera provides an enormous amount of resolution. Samsung also continues to improve its ProVisual Engine and computational processing.

My camera verdict: For best point-and-shoot photography, go for Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Battery life: Which phone lasted longer in my daily use?

The Pixel 11 Pro XL has the larger 5,115mAh battery, whereas the Galaxy S26 Ultra has a 5,000mAh battery. That difference is small, but Google is also relying on improvements in the Tensor G6 and modem efficiency to improve real-world endurance.

Google rates the Pixel 11 Pro XL for more than 30 hours of battery life and says it can reach up to 75% charge in approximately 30 minutes with a compatible 45W USB-C PPS charger.

Samsung also promises up to 75% charging in around 30 minutes with Super Fast Charging 3.0. Galaxy S26 Ultra wins on raw charging speed. You get faster 60W wired charging and reverse wired charging.

As I am more invested in wireless charging, I like Pixel more. Google’s Pixelsnap system brings magnetic accessory support and Qi2.2-certified wireless charging up to 25W. If you want to use Qi2 wireless charging with the S26 Ultra, you need a magnetic case.

My battery verdict: After testing, I found the Galaxy S26 Ultra lasts longer in daily use.

Ecosystem: Pixel vs. Samsung beyond the phone

Buying a flagship phone is rarely just about buying a phone anymore. I am also buying into an ecosystem.

The Pixel works especially well if my digital life already revolves around Google apps, services, and devices like Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch. They even work across Android, Windows, the web, tablets, and even competing smartphones.

Samsung is stronger when I already own Samsung hardware.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra integrates with:

  • Galaxy Watch
  • Galaxy Buds
  • Galaxy tablets
  • Samsung laptops
  • Samsung TVs
  • SmartThings devices

Samsung DeX also gives the Galaxy S26 Ultra a major productivity advantage. I can connect the phone to a larger display and create a desktop-like workspace. Combined with the S Pen and Samsung’s multitasking features, the Galaxy feels closer to a pocket computer than a traditional smartphone.

My ecosystem verdict: Google wins for cross-platform simplicity, but Samsung is ideal for those fully committed to Samsung hardware.

Calls, connectivity, and everyday reliability

A flagship phone can have a 200MP camera and assistive AI, but none of that matters if basic tasks are frustrating.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL benefits from Google’s spam protection and Call Assist ecosystem, along with AI-powered tools for handling calls, transcription, translation, and voice interactions.

Meanwhile, the Galaxy S26 Ultra matches the Pixel in modern connectivity options, including 5G, Wi-Fi 7, UWB, and Bluetooth 6.0.

Winner: Pixel wins communication intelligence.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Who should buy which?

At this point, I don’t think there is one universal winner. There are two very different users.

Buy the Pixel 11 Pro XL if you want:

  • The cleanest Android experience
  • Deep Gemini integration
  • Google’s Call Assist features
  • Fast Android updates
  • A simpler interface
  • Magnetic Pixelsnap accessories
  • Strong AI photography tools
  • A phone that feels smart without feeling complicated

The Pixel 11 Pro XL is the phone I would recommend to someone who wants technology to quietly help them throughout the day.

Buy the Galaxy S26 Ultra if you want:

  • The fastest Android performance
  • Better gaming performance
  • Faster wired charging
  • Dual telephoto cameras
  • An S Pen
  • Samsung DeX
  • Deep customization
  • Privacy Display
  • Local AI processing options
  • A complete Samsung ecosystem

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is the phone I would recommend to someone who wants their smartphone to do absolutely everything.

Final verdict: The Galaxy S26 Ultra is better, but I might still buy the Pixel 11 Pro XL

After going through the Pixel 11 Pro XL vs Galaxy S26 Ultra comparison, I don’t think there is a single winner for everyone.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is the more powerful and feature-packed phone. It offers faster performance, better gaming capabilities, versatile cameras, faster charging, an S Pen, and useful privacy features. If I wanted the most powerful Android phone with almost every feature imaginable, this would be my pick.

But for everyday use, I find myself leaning toward the Pixel 11 Pro XL.

Google’s phone emphasises simplicity and convenience over adding more bells and whistles. The clean software, useful Gemini integration, excellent cameras, and smart calling features make it feel effortless to use. I may not get the fastest processor or an S Pen, but I get a phone that understands what I need without overcomplicating things.

At the end of the day, both are excellent Android flagships. The better choice depends on whether you want your phone to do more or simply make your day easier.

Would you choose the feature-packed Galaxy S26 Ultra or the smarter, simpler Pixel 11 Pro XL? Let me know in the comments.

title.rendered: I stopped resizing windows manually after discovering this built-in Windows 11 trick

content.rendered:
For years, I treated manually resizing windows as an unavoidable part of multitasking on my PC. Every time working with multiple apps, I would drag one window to the side, resize another, and keep adjusting them until everything somehow fit on my screen. If you are also struggling with the same, here’s the good news. Windows 11 has solved this problem.

With Windows 11’s built-in Snap Layouts feature, you can now organize multiple windows into a clean workspace in just a few clicks or with a simple keyboard shortcut. After getting used to it, I feel that manually dragging and resizing windows is primitive.

In this guide, I will show you how to organize windows in Windows 11 using Snap Layout and share some quick tips to make multitasking easier.

What is Snap Layout on Windows 11?

Windows multitasking has always allowed basic window snapping. You could drag a window to the left or right edge of the screen and make it occupy half the display. That was useful, but Windows 11 takes the idea much further with Snap Layouts.

Instead of manually dragging and resizing every app window, Snap Layouts gives you predefined window arrangements. Depending on your screen size and resolution, you can divide your desktop into different sections and place apps exactly where you want them.

For example, you can create layouts with:

  • Two apps side by side
  • Three apps in uneven sections
  • Three equally sized columns
  • Four apps arranged in a grid

The best part is that Windows handles the sizing for you.

Microsoft has built Snap directly into Windows 11’s multitasking experience, and you can even customize features such as Snap Assist, Snap Groups, maximize-button layouts, and drag-to-snap behavior from the Multitasking settings. I think that’s what makes Snap Layouts so underrated.

How to use Snap Layouts in seconds

There are several ways to use Snap Layouts, but I have two favorites.

Method 1: Hover over the maximize button

The easiest way is almost suspiciously simple.

  1. Move your mouse over the maximize button in the top-right corner of a compatible app window.
  2. Windows 11 shows a small panel containing different Snap Layout options.
  3. From there, simply select where you want the current app to go.
  4. Windows instantly resizes the window and places it in that section of the screen.

No dragging or trying to perfectly align two windows. You can also resize the snapped windows by selecting and dragging the dividing lines.

Method 2: Press Windows + Z

Once I discovered the keyboard shortcut, I started using Snap Layouts much more often.

  1. Just press the Windows + Z key.
  2. Windows immediately displays the available Snap Layouts beneath the maximize button.
  3. Each grid in the layout has a number. Press the desired number to quickly assign a window layout.
  4. Then press the number corresponding to the zone where you want to place your active window.

To supercharge my productivity on Windows 11, I use some keyboard shortcuts for app windows. They are even faster than Snap Layout organization when you already know where you want a window.

The most useful ones are:

  • Windows + Left Arrow: Snap the active window to the left edge of your screen
  • Windows + Right Arrow: Snap the active window to the right
  • Windows + Up Arrow: Move or snap the window upward
  • Windows + Down Arrow: Move or snap the window downward
  • Esc: Disable Snap Assist

You can combine these shortcuts to move windows into corners. For example: Windows + Right Arrow > Windows + Down Arrow. This places a compatible window in the bottom-right section of the screen.

Method 3: Drag a window to the top of the screen

There’s another visual way to access Snap Layouts that I find particularly useful when I don’t want to remember a keyboard shortcut.

Simply click and hold a window by its title bar, then drag it to the top of the screen. Windows 11 will display the available Snap Layouts, allowing you to choose your preferred arrangement. You can then drag and drop the window into the exact position you want.

This method also works on touchscreen devices. Just place your finger on the window’s title bar and drag it toward the top of the screen. After the Snap Layout appears, move the window into the desired area to snap it.

It’s a simple option, but I think it’s especially useful for touchscreen laptops and tablets where keyboard shortcuts aren’t always convenient.

Snap Assist is the part that makes this feature actually useful

Snap Layouts alone would be convenient. But Snap Assist is what makes the whole experience feel genuinely intelligent.

Here’s what happens.

I snap my first app into a section of the screen. Instead of leaving the rest of the desktop empty and forcing me to manually arrange everything else, Windows shows thumbnails of my other open applications.

I can simply click one. Windows fills the next available section. Click another app to fill another section. Within a few seconds, my messy desktop becomes an organized workspace.

Snap Assist is designed to suggest other open windows after you’ve snapped one, making it easier to fill the remaining screen space without manually positioning and resizing every application one by one.

Snap Groups are the feature I didn’t know I needed

This is where Windows 11’s multitasking features became much more useful for me.

Imagine you’ve carefully arranged your workspace. Chrome is on the left; your mail inbox is on the right. Everything is perfectly organized. Then you open another application. Maybe you need to check a message on Slack or quickly open File Explorer. Normally, your carefully arranged workspace disappears behind everything else.

This is where Snap Groups come in.

Windows can remember apps that you’ve arranged together in a Snap Layout and treat them as a group. That means you can switch away from your workspace and later return to the group instead of manually rebuilding the entire layout.

Microsoft allows snapped window groups to appear when hovering over taskbar apps and through Task View (Windows Key + Tab) and Alt + Tab overlays, depending on your Snap configuration. You can switch between the Snap groups.

This is the point where I stopped thinking of Snap Layouts as a simple window-resizing feature. It’s really a lightweight workspace management tool.

Drag-and-drop still works, but I rarely use it now

To be clear, Windows hasn’t removed traditional snapping.

You can still:

  • Drag a window to the left edge
  • Drag a window to the right edge
  • Move a window toward a corner
  • Drag toward the top of the screen to access Snap options

And sometimes dragging is still convenient.

If my hands are already on the mouse and I want to quickly snap two windows together, dragging is perfectly fine. But I don’t think it’s the best method anymore.

Once you get used to Windows + Z and the arrow-key shortcuts, manually dragging windows starts feeling unnecessarily slow. Dragging requires precision, but keyboard shortcuts don’t.

Things I wish I knew before using Snap Layouts

After using Windows 11’s Snap feature more regularly, there are a few things I wish I had known sooner.

1. Your screen size changes the available layouts

Snap Layouts aren’t identical on every computer. The layouts Windows offers can depend on your display size and resolution.

Larger displays generally give you more useful multitasking options because Windows has more screen space to work with.

This makes Snap Layouts particularly enjoyable on:

  • Large monitors
  • Ultrawide displays
  • High-resolution laptops
  • Multi-monitor setups

2. You don’t have to use every Snap feature

I feel that not everyone wants Windows constantly suggesting layouts. The feature works best when you configure it to fit your workflow.

To solve this issue, Windows 11 gives you granular control over how Snap behaves. You can keep Snap enabled while disabling individual behaviors that you find distracting.

For example, you can choose whether Windows should:

  • Suggest other apps after snapping a window
  • Show Snap Layouts when hovering over the maximize button
  • Show layouts when dragging a window to the top of the screen
  • Show Snap Groups in Alt + Tab and Task View
  • Allow snapping before reaching the screen edge

These controls are available in multitasking settings. I will show them in the next section.

3. Snap Assist is better than manually filling empty space

This is probably the biggest productivity improvement.

After snapping the first window, don’t waste time dragging the second, third, and fourth windows into place. Let Snap Assist do the work.

That’s the entire point.

My favorite Snap Layouts for different types of work

Over time, I’ve started using different Snap Layouts depending on what I’m doing.

  • Writing: Two-window layout where you keep the writing window large and place the browser beside it.
  • Researching: Choose two equally sized windows. One side contains the primary source. The other contains another source, notes, or a document.
  • Multitasking: Three-window layouts are perfect for this.

I don’t use four-window layouts when working because I find too much information distracting. It’s ideal on larger displays or when you need to monitor multiple apps simultaneously.

How to customize Snap Layouts in Windows 11

If Snap Layouts don’t behave the way you want, I wouldn’t recommend turning the entire feature off immediately.

Instead, customize it.

  1. Launch Settings on your PC. Go to System from the side panel.
  2. Scroll and select Multitasking.
  3. Then expand the Snap windows section.
  4. From there, you can enable or disable individual Snap behaviors.

Microsoft’s built-in controls include options for Snap Assist suggestions, maximize-button Snap Layouts, top-of-screen Snap Layouts, Snap Groups, and edge snapping behavior.

When Snap Layouts isn’t enough, I use FancyZones

Windows 11 Snap Layouts are excellent for most people. But there is a point where the built-in layouts become limiting. This is especially true if you have an ultrawide monitor or a very specific workspace arrangement.

That’s when FancyZones, part of Microsoft PowerToys, becomes worth considering. Unlike the predefined Snap layouts in Windows 11, FancyZones lets you divide your screen exactly the way you want. You can create multiple custom layouts for different workflows and quickly switch between them using keyboard shortcuts.

Once you install PowerToys, the feature is enabled by default; no setup required. To start snapping windows, simply hold down the Shift key while dragging a window. Your custom zones will appear, and you can drop the window into the section you want.

You can also customize the keyboard shortcuts and mouse actions that trigger FancyZones directly from the PowerToys settings. This gives you far more control over how windows behave compared to the standard Snap Layouts feature.

However, I wouldn’t recommend installing it just because you can. For most users, Windows 11’s built-in Snap Layouts are enough. But if you’ve reached the point where you’re constantly thinking, “I wish I could divide my screen exactly this way,” FancyZones is the logical next step.

Stop wasting time resizing windows!

Snap Layouts may seem like a small Windows 11 feature, but it can make multitasking much easier. Instead of constantly dragging and resizing windows, I can organize my apps in seconds using a layout that fits what I’m working on.

Whether you prefer using the maximize button, the keyboard shortcut, or simply dragging a window to the top of the screen, there are plenty of easy ways to get started. And if the built-in layouts aren’t flexible enough, FancyZones gives you even more control.

So, how do you manage multiple windows on your PC? Are you a Snap Layouts user, or do you still prefer manually arranging your desktop? I’d love to know which method works best for you.

title.rendered: Asahi Linux now supports M3 Macs, but GPU support is still missing

content.rendered:
Asahi Linux now officially supports Macs with M3, M3 Pro, and M3 Max chips. The project merged M3 support into its installer on September 6, giving owners of newer Apple silicon Macs a supported path to try Linux.

This is a major compatibility step, not a finished desktop Linux port. Asahi says most of the hardware support already available on M1 and M2 now works on M3, but GPU and full display-controller support remain unfinished.

The core Mac hardware is working

Asahi says M3 support includes the webcam, internal microphones, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB up to the hardware’s 10 Gb/s limit, and hardware-accelerated video decoding with AV1 support. The M3 feature-support table breaks down the status for individual Mac models and components.

The rollout covers M3, M3 Pro, and M3 Max Macs. If you are comparing those chips before trying Linux, this M3, M3 Pro, and M3 Max comparison explains where the hardware tiers differ.

The important limits are graphics and sleep

The biggest problem is the GPU. Asahi warns that users should not expect performant or power-efficient 3D acceleration yet, which makes this release a poor fit for graphics-heavy work or gaming.

There are a few other practical limits:

  • Sleep does not work because of limitations with the firmware-provided framebuffer.
  • The HDMI port on MacBooks that have one is disabled until full display-controller support arrives.
  • The M3 Ultra Mac Studio is not supported yet.
  • M3 installation is behind the installer’s Expert mode while the work is still fresh.

Asahi hopes to remove the Expert-mode requirement around the Fedora Linux 45 beta in a couple of weeks, provided testing does not uncover major regressions. The project has not promised a date for GPU or full display-controller support.

Should you install Asahi Linux on an M3 Mac?

Linux enthusiasts who can live with broken sleep, missing HDMI output, and unfinished graphics now have a genuine way to test Asahi on M3 hardware. For a daily driver, it makes more sense to wait until GPU and display support are further along.

The same M3 Macs already run Apple’s current software. This macOS Golden Gate compatibility list can help you check the official macOS path before deciding whether the early Asahi release fits your needs.

excerpt.rendered: Asahi Linux has added M3, M3 Pro, and M3 Max Macs to its installer. The release works on much of the hardware but still lacks usable GPU and full display support.

title.rendered: Apple may change App Store rules to raise revenue, report says

content.rendered:
Apple may be preparing a new push to make the App Store more profitable. In the latest Power On newsletter, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that CEO John Ternus and services chief Eddy Cue are looking for ways to improve App Store margins and add more recurring revenue.

No policy has changed yet. Gurman’s report does not name a finished proposal, so developers and iPhone users have nothing new to change today.

The possible changes are still unclear

The report does not say whether Apple will change commission rates, developer fees, or App Review. Possible routes include a higher annual developer membership, recurring charges for large apps that generate heavy traffic, or more automated app review to reduce operating costs. Those are scenarios, not announced Apple plans.

Apple currently charges $99 per membership year for the Apple Developer Program. Raising that fee would affect developers who distribute apps, while a traffic-based charge would target larger services. More automated review could lower costs, but it would also raise questions about whether Apple can maintain the same level of safety and quality checks.

Why the App Store is back in focus

Apple’s Services business reached a record $30.7 billion in fiscal Q3 2026. During the earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh said App Store business-model changes in some countries, the U.S. link-out ruling, and weaker mobile gaming affected the store’s performance. Apple’s results confirm the record quarter, while the earlier App Store update breaks down the comments about those headwinds.

The App Store is only one part of Services, and Apple does not report its revenue as a separate line. Still, it is a high-volume platform with recurring payments, which makes even small changes to fees or review costs meaningful to Apple’s margins.

Phil Schiller’s exit adds context

Gurman also links the App Store debate to Phil Schiller’s decision to step away from overseeing the store and Apple’s product launches. Schiller reportedly believed that trying to squeeze more profit from the platform could further irritate developers and governments. Apple still lists him as an Apple Fellow, and the revenue strategy is only one reported factor in his move.

That tension is familiar. Apple is under pressure to grow Services, while developers and regulators continue to challenge the fees and rules that make the App Store so profitable. Recent App Review changes around stale copycat apps show how the company is already adjusting the store’s rules in other areas.

Nothing changes for developers yet

The current $99 membership price and existing App Store terms remain in place. Until Apple publishes a new agreement or announces a specific change, developers do not need to update their pricing or distribution plans because of this report.

For now, this is a signal about the direction Ternus and Cue may want to take, not a new App Store rule. The next meaningful update will be a concrete proposal, especially if it affects developer fees, app review, or payments.

excerpt.rendered: Apple is reportedly exploring ways to make the App Store more profitable under John Ternus and Eddy Cue, but no new fees or policies are confirmed yet.

title.rendered: CarPlay now supports five major AI chatbots, including Claude

content.rendered:
CarPlay now has a fifth major AI chatbot. 9to5Mac reports that Anthropic’s latest Claude iPhone app update adds CarPlay support, joining ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok, and Meta AI.

Apple opened CarPlay to voice-based conversational apps with iOS 26.4. The earlier iOS 26.4 CarPlay update detailed the voice-first category, which Apple’s CarPlay developer page now lists alongside navigation, audio, messaging, and EV charging apps. Apple’s iOS 27 beta is also expected to bring Siri AI into the car, so third-party chatbots are arriving before Apple’s own assistant gets there.

Claude’s CarPlay experience is voice-first

Claude’s CarPlay interface focuses on the parts that make sense behind the wheel. It shows recent chats you can resume and lets you start a new voice conversation from the car’s display. You are not getting the full Claude app with all of its document, image, and project controls.

The format is closer to a hands-free chat window than a replacement for Apple’s system assistant. OpenAI’s ChatGPT CarPlay guidance makes the boundary clear for its own app: CarPlay cannot access maps, vehicle information, live location, or control other apps. A ChatGPT CarPlay hands-on shows why these apps still feel separate from Siri. Claude’s update is presented in the same voice-focused lane.

The current lineup has five apps

The major chatbot apps now reported to work with CarPlay are:

  • ChatGPT
  • Perplexity
  • Grok
  • Meta AI
  • Claude

This gives drivers more choice for quick questions or ongoing voice conversations, but each app remains a separate CarPlay experience. The report describes chat and voice features, not a new layer for changing the car’s settings, starting navigation, or managing the rest of the iPhone.

What you need to use Claude in CarPlay

You need an iPhone running iOS 26.4 or later, the latest Claude app, and a car that supports CarPlay. After the app update reaches your iPhone, Claude should appear with the other compatible apps in CarPlay.

Apple’s rules keep these apps focused on voice interaction and a small number of car-friendly controls. That is useful for asking a question without reaching for the phone, but it also means you still need Apple’s built-in apps for navigation, messages, music, and vehicle features.

Claude’s arrival widens the AI choice inside CarPlay just as Siri AI approaches iOS 27. For now, these services are voice-first additions to the dashboard, not full replacements for Siri’s system access.

title.rendered: I finally stopped Google Maps from changing my shared route

content.rendered:
I always assumed that if I selected a route in Google Maps and shared it with someone, they would see the exact same route. But that wasn’t always the case. Google Maps would sometimes suggest a completely different path, ignoring the shared route.

It was most irritating when I was planning a scenic drive and wanted to avoid certain roads.. After experimenting with different options, I found a simple trick that stops Google Maps from changing my route.

Here’s how to keep Google Maps on a specific route.

Why Google Maps changes shared routes

Here’s the biggest misconception I had: choosing a route isn’t the same as locking a route. When Google Maps shows multiple ways to reach a destination, it lets you select the one you prefer. Naturally, I assumed that the selection would only be shown when I shared it.

But Google Maps is fundamentally designed for dynamic navigation. It continuously evaluates traffic, road conditions, closures, and other factors that might make another route more efficient. So when someone opens a shared Google Maps route, the app can still recalculate the journey.

Normally, that’s actually useful. If there’s a major accident ahead, I don’t want Google Maps blindly following an outdated plan just because I selected that road three hours ago. But things become problematic when the route is important.

Imagine planning a scenic road trip. You deliberately choose a beautiful route through small towns and viewpoints. Google Maps then decides that a boring highway will save 12 minutes. Technically, Google Maps did its job. But it completely missed the point.

The same thing happens when you:

  • Want to avoid a stressful highway.
  • Know a particular road is easier to drive.
  • Plan a motorcycle ride.
  • Want everyone in a convoy to follow roughly the same path.
  • Need to pass through specific towns.
  • Prefer a familiar route over Google’s suggested shortcut.

Google Maps is excellent at answering, “What’s the fastest way to get there?” But sometimes that’s not the question I’m asking.

The simple trick that finally worked: Adding stops along the way

The solution was surprisingly obvious once I understood how Google Maps thinks. Instead of creating a route with the starting and final destination points, you need to create something more like this: Start → Stop 1 → Stop 2 → Final Destination. Those extra stops act as strategic waypoints.

Google Maps now has to calculate a journey that reaches those locations. It still has the freedom to choose roads between them, but it has significantly less freedom to suddenly send the entire trip in a completely different direction. We will see how to customize and lock a Google Maps route in the next section.

Let’s say you are planning a trip between two cities but specifically want to avoid the toll highway. In that case, I will add one or two towns along that custom route as intermediate stops, rather than endlessly trying to force Maps onto the preferred route.

Now the navigation can’t simply ignore those places and send you straight down the highway. The route has to pass through them. The best part is that the stops don’t necessarily have to be places where you plan to spend time. Sometimes, they’re simply guideposts.

How do I choose the right waypoints?

If you add a stop point every few kilometers, your route becomes unnecessarily complicated. The goal isn’t to micromanage Google Maps into following every turn. It’s to give it just enough direction to keep it close to your intended route.

I’ve found that the best waypoints are the ones placed at decision points. These are the places where Maps is most likely to betray my original plan.

For example, I look for:

  • A town I specifically want to pass through: If Maps keeps trying to route me around a town, I simply add that town as an intermediate stop. Now it becomes part of the journey rather than an optional detour.
  • A point before an unwanted highway: Google Maps might follow your preferred road for most of the journey before suddenly rerouting you onto a highway. In that case, add a waypoint shortly before the point.
  • A landmark on the scenic route: I always add a viewpoint, popular attraction, café, petrol station, or other landmark along the road I plan to take. Even if I don’t plan to stop there for long, it helps anchor the route in the right direction.
  • A major junction: Sometimes you don’t care about the exact road leading to or from a location. A strategically placed waypoint near a major junction can be enough to keep the route on track.

My simple rule is to add the minimum number of stops needed to influence the journey. If you are confused, you can use the Gemini AI-powered Ask Maps feature for route-planning tips.

How to set up a shareable route that stays on track

Once you start using waypoints, making Google Maps follow a specific route becomes pretty straightforward.

Here’s the process I use:

  1. Open Google Maps and tap the navigation icon.
  2. Now, enter your starting point and final destination as usual.
  3. Google Maps will suggest multiple routes. You may customize it by selecting options such as Avoid tolls and Avoid highways. Now, choose the route that makes sense for you.
  4. Tap Add stops at the bottom.
  5. Maps suggests Points of interest and Top restaurants along the way. Choose among them or search for a location you want to drive by.
  6. Repeat the above step to add multiple stops in order.
  7. Now, review the entire route to avoid an unnecessary detour.
  8. Once the route includes your key waypoints, tap the share button and send the directions to your family or friends.

When they open the link, Google Maps will show the multi-stop route you created.

This isn’t a perfect route lock, and that’s actually okay

I want to be very clear about one thing: adding stops does not permanently lock Google Maps onto every road you choose. And honestly, you wouldn’t want it to. If a road suddenly closes, it will be a no-brainer for Google Maps to stubbornly insist on driving into a barricade just because you planned that route yesterday.

Navigation needs flexibility. So, even with intermediate stops, Google Maps can still respond to:

  • Traffic jams
  • Road closures
  • Accidents
  • Construction
  • Temporary restrictions
  • Changing road conditions

But because the app still needs to reach my chosen waypoints, the overall journey is much more likely to stay close to my original plan.

When should you use this trick?

I don’t use waypoints for every Google Maps journey. If you’re commuting somewhere familiar or simply want the fastest route, follow Google Maps rerouting suggestions.

But I absolutely use this trick when the journey matters as much as the destination.

  • Scenic road trips: If you’re planning a road trip specifically to enjoy the drive, don’t let Google Maps optimize all the interesting parts out of it.
  • Group drives and convoys: When multiple people are driving separately, sharing a route with strategic waypoints gives everyone a clearer structure to follow.
  • Motorcycle rides: The curves, roads, scenery, and stops are often the entire reason for the ride. Therefore, letting an algorithm constantly optimize the route for speed makes very little sense.
  • Avoiding roads you don’t want to take: Maybe there’s a highway you dislike or a particular road is stressful to drive on. Waypoints along the way save you from having to manually navigate every turn.
  • Routes through specific towns: If I need to pass through a particular town for food, fuel, sightseeing, or any other reason, adding it as a stop makes the route much more predictable.

Prevent Google Maps from rerouting!

Google Maps is great at finding the fastest route, but the fastest route isn’t always the one you want to take. I learned that simply selecting a route doesn’t guarantee that it will stay the same when I share it.

Adding a few strategic stops along the way is a simple workaround that gives you more control over the journey. It doesn’t completely lock the route, but it makes it much harder for Google Maps to take the trip in a completely different direction.

Have you ever had Google Maps completely change a route you carefully planned? I’d love to know how you dealt with it.

content.rendered:
Update: Verified the latest Giant Simulator Reborn Codes on October 01, 2026

Giant Simulator: Reborn starts you small and makes every click, weapon, pet, and rebirth matter. Gold pays for gear and pets, while Embers and Soul Gems support newer event and progression systems. The newest codes give you Embers and potion bundles before you start tapping your way up the leaderboard. Redeem them exactly as shown, then rejoin if a fresh code refuses to load.

All working Giant Simulator Reborn codes

  • EMBERS: 500 embers (NEW)
  • LAVA: 500 embers (NEW)
  • CLANS: Free potions
  • SUMMERGEM: Redeem this code for a 2x Soul Gem Potion

Expired Giant Simulator Reborn codes

Demonking, Razorfishpets, Gianttofuu, Planetmilopets, Freegold, Azadpets, and Pets

How to redeem Giant Simulator Reborn codes

The code menu sits behind the white bird icon on the right side of the screen.

  1. Open Giant Simulator: REBORN on Roblox.
  2. Click the Codes option on the left side of the screen.
  3. Paste a working code into the Enter Code box.
  4. Click Collect to claim the reward. If your version shows Enter, use that button instead.

Why your Giant Simulator Reborn code is not working

AZADPETS, DEMONKING, FREEGOLD, GIANTTOFUU, PETS, PLANETMILOPETS, RAZORFISHPETS

If a new code fails, leave the experience and join a different server. That is usually faster than repeatedly submitting the same string in an old session.

Where to find more Giant Simulator Reborn codes

New codes tend to arrive with events, updates, milestones, and developer announcements. Check the Giant Simulator: REBORN Roblox page, the Mithril Games Roblox group, the official Mithril Games Discord, and Mithril Games on X when a new event begins.

The Discord is usually the quickest place to see a fresh code, but bookmarking this page saves you from testing old Gold strings one by one.

Must read:

  • Rogue Piece Rebirth codes
  • Roll a Fisherman codes
  • Fabled Legacy codes

title.rendered: How to get the Cheat Master Storm Scout Sprite in Fortnite

content.rendered:
Fortnite Override recently added its first new sprite, on top of the ones rolled out at launch, with the introduction of Storm Scout Sprite. Equipping it gives you a temporary overdrive effect after you take a certain amount of storm damage in the match. While this particular sprite may not exactly be rare, its Cheat Master variant is sort of hard to come across.

A majority of Cheat Master variant sprites can be easily unlocked by using Fortnite admin panel codes or lobby hacks from the home screen. However, the same method doesn’t apply to Cheat Master Storm Scout sprite as there is no code that grants you this item, making it a relatively rare sprite compared to other Cheat Master sprites.

Below, you can check out all the ways that you can actually try to get your hands on Cheat Master Storm Scout Sprite. Additionally, the locations where this sprite has been encountered by streamers before have also been compiled in this article.

Ways to get Cheat Master Storm Scout Sprite in Fortnite

Opening chests

As is obvious, the most traditional way of hunting for a sprite is by scouring the Battle Royale map for chests, specifically the blue Rare Chests. In the new map, Stone Sanctum, the maze to its south-east, and the three Pac-Man islands (located at the north, south-west, and south-east tips of the island) are the key points of interest where high-tier chests are commonly scattered throughout. Besides that, Cluster Coast and Golden Grove are also known to house highly rewarding chests.

Entering cheat codes

In Fortnite Override, cheat codes were introduced as interactive interfaces where you need to press your d-pad in a given order to unlock a sprite. They come in multiple different types, ranging from blue cheat codes that offer a rare sprite to yellow ones that offer a mythic sprite. There are a multitude of these cheat codes available throughout the in-game map.

You can get any rare sprite, including the Cheat Master Storm Scout Sprite, relatively quick by focusing on map locations most concentrated with cheat codes. As per Fortnite.gg, the top-three places that meet such a requirement are Heatwave Harbor, Cluster Coast, and Shaken Sanctuary. Moreover, the parts surrounding the center of the map are also fairly abundant in terms of cheat codes.

You may also use a Cheat Code Locator, available for purchase for 1,500 Sprite Dust at in-game Extraction Sites, to reveal the locations of cheat codes on the map. But before that, don’t forget to claim a total of four such items for free by entering “FindItChat” and “SurviveTheNight” Lobby Hacks into the admin panel.

Indexing from a friend

If none of the above methods work or you just want this sprite the easier way, you can try indexing it from another Fortnite player. There are some players on the game’s official Discord who are willing to share their sprite with others.

Once you find someone like that, join a match together and, when they drop the desired sprite for you, extract the same. Doing so will index the sprite into your Sprite collection. In the next game, you can return the sprite to its original owner and use Sprite Dust to regenerate your own.

Rounding up

Fortnite devs leaving Cheat Master Storm Scout Sprite from their lobby hacks list does make it quite a rare possession. However, the prevalence of cheat codes in the Fortnite Override map ensures that players have a reasonable chance to find this sprite.

Besides this one sprite, there are a few more that players would be busy catching in the coming days, thanks to the rollout of Fortnite v42.10 update on Thursday. The latest content drop added fan-made sprites such as the Onigiri Sprite and IP-inspired ones such as the Mega Man Sprite, breathing new life into the sprite hunt this season.

title.rendered: Why Windows 11 keeps asking for a Microsoft account: I finally found the truth

content.rendered:
Every time I set up a new Windows 11 PC, I run into the same thing: Microsoft asking me to sign in with a Microsoft account. And it’s not just during setup. Windows regularly nudges me to sign in, sync my files, back up my data, and connect to Microsoft’s services.

At first, I assumed Microsoft simply wanted more of my data. But after digging deeper into why Windows 11 keeps asking for a Microsoft account, I found that the truth was much less dramatic and far more practical. Here’s why Microsoft pushes its account so heavily, how it differs from a local account, and whether you actually need one on your Windows 11 PC.

Why does Windows 11 keep asking for a Microsoft account?

The short answer is that a Microsoft account turns a standalone Windows PC into part of Microsoft’s much larger ecosystem.

A local account is simple. I create a username and password, sign in to my computer, and the account essentially lives on that device. Windows works, my files stay on my PC unless I choose to upload them elsewhere, and I can decide which online services I want to use separately.

A Microsoft account changes that relationship. The same account can connect Windows with:

  • OneDrive
  • Microsoft 365
  • Outlook
  • Xbox
  • Microsoft Store purchases
  • Copilot
  • Cloud backups
  • Cross-device syncing
  • Windows activation

That’s when the constant sign-in reminders started making more sense to me. Microsoft isn’t repeatedly asking me to sign in because Windows suddenly can’t function without my email address. It wants Windows connected to the broader Microsoft ecosystem.

I initially thought it was all about data collection

My first assumption was that Microsoft’s push toward Microsoft accounts was mainly about data collection.

Windows 11 already collects diagnostic data, commonly referred to as telemetry, to help Microsoft understand how devices perform, identify bugs, improve Windows, and troubleshoot problems. So naturally, I wondered: if Windows is already collecting diagnostic information, why does it also want me to sign in with a Microsoft account?

That’s part of what makes the Microsoft account requirement uncomfortable for privacy-conscious users.

However, Windows diagnostic data and your Microsoft account aren’t exactly the same thing. Windows can collect required diagnostic information regardless of whether you’re using a local or Microsoft account.

A Microsoft account instead provides a persistent identity that works across Microsoft’s products and services. The same account can be used with Windows, Outlook, OneDrive, Xbox, Microsoft 365, and other Microsoft products.

So, while privacy is still a valid consideration, there’s more behind Microsoft’s account push than simply collecting Windows telemetry.

The boring truth behind why Windows 11 needs a Microsoft account

Microsoft isn’t pushing a Microsoft account because it desperately needs my email address. It wants the relationship with its wider ecosystem that comes with it.

1. Microsoft wants Windows connected to its entire ecosystem

This is the biggest reason, in my opinion. A Microsoft account isn’t really just a Windows login anymore. It’s Microsoft’s universal membership card.

When I sign in to Windows with one, it gives me access to a vast number of services without creating individual accounts for them. So, my files, settings, purchases in Outlook, Office, OneDrive, Skype, Xbox, and Windows remain synced across devices.

That’s convenient.

2. Cloud backup makes Microsoft accounts more valuable

I used to dismiss cloud backup as one of those features companies aggressively pushed to get me to buy another subscription. However, when I moved from an old PC to a new one, it was irritating to recreate years of settings and preferences. Then I understood why Microsoft wants Windows users connected to cloud services.

Sometimes, computers fail, drives die, laptops get stolen, or people accidentally delete files. With a local account, you would have no way to restore the previous configuration. With a Microsoft account, my digital identity and Windows experience can move with me.

Windows Backup stores settings, personalization, Wi-Fi passwords, language preferences, installed apps, and supported folders through OneDrive under a Microsoft account. So, when you set up a new PC or reinstall Windows and sign in with the same account, everything gets restored.

3. Your Windows license is another reason to sign in

This was the part that made Microsoft’s argument more convincing to me. A Microsoft account isn’t just useful for apps and cloud services. It can also help connect my Windows digital license to my identity.

Linking a Microsoft account with a Windows digital license can make reactivation easier after a significant hardware change, for instance, replacing your motherboard. This may seem like a rare case until it happens to you.

Imagine replacing a major hardware component and suddenly having to convince Windows that, yes, this is still your computer. Having an account associated with the digital license can make that process easier through Microsoft’s Activation troubleshooter.

4. Windows is the gateway to Microsoft’s other services

Windows isn’t Microsoft’s only business anymore. It has Microsoft 365 subscriptions, cloud storage, gaming, AI products, business software, developer tools, and more.

Windows is one of the biggest doors into that universe. And if Microsoft can get me signed in at the operating system level, it has created the perfect starting point for introducing everything else.

  • Need cloud storage? Here’s OneDrive.
  • Need productivity apps? Microsoft 365 is right there.
  • Want AI assistance? Copilot is built into the Windows experience.
  • Want games? There’s Xbox integration.
  • Need apps? The Microsoft Store is waiting.

It’s simply ecosystem strategy.

How to install and log in to Windows 11 without a Microsoft account

Connecting a Microsoft account to your Windows 11 can genuinely make life easier. But that doesn’t mean a Microsoft account is the right choice for everyone.

A local account gives me a simpler and more independent Windows experience. I don’t have to connect my PC login to my cloud storage, email, Xbox profile, or other Microsoft services. My account stays on the device, and I decide exactly which services I want to connect.

If that’s the experience you prefer, you can still set up Windows 11 with a local account.

  1. Start setting up Windows 11 by following the on-screen instructions.
  2. Continue until you reach the Microsoft account sign-in screen. Then press Shift + F10 to open Command Prompt.
  3. There enter: start ms-cxh:localonly
  4. Windows should open a Create a user for this PC window. Now create a local username and password and continue the setup without signing in to a Microsoft account.

Alternatively, you can create a Windows installation USB using Rufus, which offers options to remove the Microsoft account requirement during setup.

However, if you have already installed Windows 11, you don’t need to reinstall Windows just to get rid of the Microsoft account.

  1. Open Settings and go to Accounts > Your info.
  2. Select Sign in with a local account instead, then follow the prompts to complete the switch.
  3. Go back to Accounts and select Sign-in Options.
  4. Click the dropdown next to When should Windows require you to sign-in again and set it to Never.

This ensures you won’t have to log in every time you wake your PC or make changes.

Final thoughts

After looking into it, I realized the reason Windows 11 keeps pushing a Microsoft account isn’t particularly mysterious. Microsoft wants to connect Windows with the rest of its ecosystem, making it easier to sync settings, back up files, restore a PC, and access services like OneDrive and Microsoft 365.

But some users prefer a simple local account without connecting their PC to Microsoft’s wider ecosystem. Fortunately, that option still exists. In the end, I don’t think Microsoft accounts are the problem. I just think users should be able to decide how connected they want their Windows experience to be.

  • How to make Windows 11 actually shut down completely

title.rendered: Apple may add a 13.8-inch OLED MacBook between the Air and Pro

content.rendered:
Apple may be planning a new 13.8-inch OLED MacBook for around 2029, according to an updated Omdia display roadmap. The machine would sit between the LCD MacBook Air and the higher-end OLED MacBook Pro, creating a fourth MacBook category if Apple takes the plan forward.

This is a roadmap prediction, not a product announcement. Apple has not confirmed the MacBook, its name, its price, or a launch date.

The 13.8-inch model could fill a gap in Apple’s lineup

The current MacBook sizes leave a narrow space between the 13.6-inch MacBook Air and 14.2-inch MacBook Pro. Apple also sells the 13-inch MacBook Neo at the budget end. A 13.8-inch model would be close to the Air in size, but its OLED screen could give it a clearer reason to cost more.

Omdia’s updated roadmap reportedly separates the 13.8-inch MacBook from the MacBook Air rather than simply listing it as an OLED Air. That points to a new middle tier, although the product category could still change before 2029.

There is some earlier evidence that Apple has explored the idea. In June, ZDNet Korea reported that Apple sent requests for information about a 13.8-inch OLED MacBook panel to Samsung Display, LG Display, and BOE. An RFI is an early technical information-gathering step that comes before a formal quote request, so it does not mean production is locked in.

ZDNet Korea described two possible outcomes at the time. Apple could introduce a new product between the Air and Pro, or it could adjust the Air’s screen size from 13.6 inches to 13.8 inches. Omdia’s later roadmap favors the separate-model interpretation, but Apple’s final lineup is still unknown.

The panel would sit below the OLED MacBook Pro

The rumored 13.8-inch machine would use a single-stack hybrid OLED panel. Apple’s upcoming Pro models are expected to use a more expensive tandem OLED design. That difference would let Apple bring OLED contrast and deeper blacks to a less expensive MacBook without matching the Pro’s display hardware.

Omdia’s panel roadmap also lists an LTPO+ backplane, integrated touch sensing, an under-panel camera, and a color filter built into the OLED encapsulation layer. Those features could lead to a thinner display assembly, a touchscreen, and a smaller or invisible camera cutout, but they are not confirmed MacBook specifications.

The premium side of the plan is already being tracked in reports about Apple’s OLED MacBook Pro redesign. The rumored middle model would use a less advanced panel and could give Apple a way to separate the two tiers by display quality as well as performance.

The MacBook Air may stay on LCD for longer

Omdia’s roadmap shows the MacBook Air continuing with LCD panels into 2030. If that projection holds, Apple would use the new 13.8-inch machine to bring OLED to more buyers while keeping the Air cheaper and simpler.

That would make the lineup easier to understand in one way and more crowded in another. The Air would remain the mainstream choice, the new MacBook would offer a premium display and possibly touch, and the Pro would keep the highest-end screen and performance options. The current MacBook Pro design dates back to 2021, so Apple has room to use a new display tier to mark a wider redesign.

The timeline leaves plenty of room for change. Panel costs, manufacturing capacity, and demand for touch-enabled Macs could all alter the plan before 2029. For now, the 13.8-inch OLED MacBook is best understood as a possible new rung between Apple’s Air and Pro lines, not a MacBook you can expect to buy soon.

title.rendered: GPT-6 Astra brings faster computer use and searchable context to ChatGPT and Codex

content.rendered:
OpenAI has officially launched GPT-6 Astra, its new flagship model for computer use, coding, browsing, science, and professional work. The rollout starts with a limited set of organizations before expanding to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users over the next few days.

The most useful changes are aimed at long, messy tasks. ChatGPT can work through more steps on a computer, while Codex can keep track of earlier context instead of relying only on a compressed summary when a session runs long.

Astra is built to work across a computer

OpenAI says Astra can fill out forms, update customer records, organize calendars, research online, edit documents, build spreadsheets and presentations, create websites, and run frontend checks. These are OpenAI’s stated capabilities and examples, not independent test results.

The company reports a 72.6% score for Astra on OSWorld 2.0, compared with 65.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI also says Astra completed the simulated tasks in about 40 minutes, versus about 75 minutes for Sol. That works out to roughly 47% less time per task in the company’s test.

OpenAI has updated the Codex harness alongside the model. On the Mind2Web benchmark, it says Astra and the new harness completed tasks 1.9 times faster than the current GPT-5.6 Sol experience. The combination matters because computer-use models spend a lot of time reading screens, deciding what to click, and recovering from small changes in an interface.

The focus follows the recent GPT-5.5 upgrade for ChatGPT and Codex, which pushed OpenAI’s coding tools toward longer tasks that include investigation, testing, and revision.

Codex can search earlier context windows

Codex is getting a more specific context feature with Astra. When a long session fills its context window, Astra can keep notes across windows instead of repeatedly reducing the work to one summary. Earlier context windows also remain searchable, so Codex can retrieve a requirement, failed test, or tool result that did not make it into the notes.

That should help with large refactors and difficult debugging sessions, where the reason behind a failed fix can be as important as the fix itself. OpenAI says the feature is experimental now. Users can enable it in Codex, and it will become the default for Astra in the coming weeks.

It also fits the way OpenAI has been spreading Codex across devices. The Codex experience on iPhone and Android lets users check work and steer a session away from the computer, while Astra is aimed at keeping the session coherent when the work itself gets longer.

The rollout is gradual because Astra is more capable

OpenAI says Astra is its first model to reach the Critical level of cybersecurity capability under its Preparedness Framework. Its safety overview says the model can find unknown security flaws and develop exploits with the right tools and access, so the company has added stronger safeguards and broad misalignment monitoring.

The model is also being tested against prompt injection and destructive computer actions such as unauthorized transactions, data loss, or excessive access. If the monitoring system detects a possible problem, ChatGPT or Codex may pause or stop the task so the user can review it.

That extra friction is part of the launch. Astra may be better at operating a computer, but it is also being given more ways to affect the user’s files, accounts, and browser sessions.

When GPT-6 Astra will be available

OpenAI says Astra is rolling out first to a limited set of organizations. Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users are next, with access also coming to the OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure, and AWS Bedrock. Enterprise administrators must enable it, and access is off by default at launch.

Developers can use the gpt-6-astra model ID. OpenAI lists standard API pricing at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fast mode can run at up to twice the speed for twice the standard price.

The ChatGPT app on Mac remains the most natural place to see the computer-use side of Astra, but access will depend on the account, plan, and rollout stage. For now, GPT-6 Astra is a controlled release of a more capable agent, not an instant replacement for every ChatGPT model.
